topic.title: Setting the cleaning arrangement for the shared areas
topic.context: Five housemates share a kitchen, a bathroom, and a living room, and the informal habit they started with has stopped working. They are settling on one arrangement for the coming year.

options.label: A
options.name: Fixed Weekly Rota
options.summary: Each area is assigned to one person for a named week, rotating through the household in a published order that repeats until someone asks for it to be revised.

options.label: B
options.name: Paid Cleaning Service
options.summary: An outside cleaner comes on a set schedule for the shared areas, with the household handling the arrangements and settling the invoice among themselves each month.

options.label: C
options.name: Standing Assignments
options.summary: Each person takes permanent ownership of particular areas for as long as they live there, choosing their own timing rather than following a shared calendar.

problems.1: The bleach, the bin bags and the sponges keep coming out of whoever's wallet is nearest, and nobody has settled up since spring. Whatever we agree to, I want to know what it costs us month to month and who ends up out of pocket in the meantime.
problems.2: Every one of these rooms takes longer than anyone admits, and the stretches when it all lands at once are the stretches I get nothing else done. Before we commit for a year I want to know what the hours really look like, and whether handing them off actually removes them.
problems.3: The bathroom is the room I brace myself before walking into, and the kitchen is fine one day and grim the next with no pattern I can see. I would like to stop having to guess what state a room will be in.
problems.4: It has stopped feeling even — the same rooms seem to land on the same people, and someone who is hardly ever here counts the same as someone who never leaves. I want to see where the using and the work actually sit before we fix anything for a year.
problems.5: Nobody here wants to be the one who brings the kitchen up again, so it goes unsaid until it comes out sideways at someone. Whatever we settle on, I care more about which version leaves us on speaking terms a year from now than about the rooms themselves.

topic.title: Choosing the destination for the club's training camp
topic.context: A university club runs one training camp a year, and the five members organizing it must commit to a destination before bookings open. The whole membership will travel together.

options.label: A
options.name: Coastal Lodge
options.summary: A seaside guesthouse two prefectures away that the club has never used, offering the group its own building and meals arranged through the owner.

options.label: B
options.name: Mountain Training Centre
options.summary: A public sports facility inland with shared dormitories and equipment on site, booked through the municipal reservation system.

options.label: C
options.name: Campus Intensive
options.summary: A block of consecutive days in the club's own facilities on campus, with accommodation arranged separately for members who live too far to commute.

problems.1: The fee we announced for last year's camp came up short of what the trip actually cost, and the club account has been carrying the gap ever since. I am not putting a number in front of the membership again until I know where the money really goes.
problems.2: Whoever ran last year's camp lost most of a month of evenings to the arrangements and then spent the camp itself on duty instead of training. Two of those people have already said they will not take it on a second time.
problems.3: Half the group came back from the last camp having slept badly for four nights running, and the final day's sessions were visibly worse for it. Before anything is booked I want to know what the nights and the days would actually be like.
problems.4: The camp goes out at one flat fee, and I suspect it lands very unevenly once what people spend on the side is counted. When someone pulls out at the last minute, we have also never worked out whose money covers it.
problems.5: The club has drifted into year-groups that barely speak outside practice, and the last camp did nothing to change that. Where we go decides who spends their evenings with whom — and who turns up at all.

topic.title: Reorganizing the neighbourhood refuse point
topic.context: The collection point that five neighbouring households share has become a recurring source of complaints. The five representatives are settling on one arrangement with the ward office.

options.label: A
options.name: Enclosed Structure
options.summary: A permanent enclosure is built at the existing location, with the households handling the ward application and the construction arrangements themselves.

options.label: B
options.name: Rotating Location
options.summary: The point moves between the frontages of the participating households on a published rotation, changing at fixed intervals through the year.

options.label: C
options.name: Managed Collection Hours
options.summary: The point stays where it is, but refuse may only be put out inside a narrow window before collection, with the households taking turns to oversee it.

problems.1: Whatever we settle on, the bill lands on five households with very different room in their budgets, and so far nobody has added up either what it would take to set up or what this corner already costs us every year.
problems.2: Every arrangement this lane has agreed to has ended up resting on whoever answers the phone first, and I have watched that quietly wear people down. Before we commit I want to know, in hours, what this one takes out of us — the setting up and the keeping it going.
problems.3: The corner has stopped being somewhere anyone wants to walk past in August, and I suspect the obvious fix would only swap one daily annoyance for another. I wanted to know what each of these arrangements is really like to live beside, morning by morning.
problems.4: One household has had this at their gate for years while the rest of us only walk past it, and I do not want us to sign something that quietly leaves it that way. Any plan that calls itself equal deserves a hard look at what each of us would actually be taking on.
problems.5: Two of these households have barely spoken since the last row about the bins, and whatever we choose, we still have to live on this lane together. What worries me is less which arrangement wins than which one leaves us able to knock on each other's doors afterwards.

topic.title: Rearranging the office seating
topic.context: A team of five has outgrown the way its desks were originally placed, and the layout is being settled before the floor is reorganized. All five will sit in whatever is decided.

options.label: A
options.name: Fixed Desks by Function
options.summary: Desks are grouped by the kind of work each person does, with each seat permanently assigned and named on the floor plan.

options.label: B
options.name: Free Address
options.summary: No seat belongs to anyone; people take whatever desk is open when they arrive and clear it before leaving at the end of the day.

options.label: C
options.name: Rotating Blocks
options.summary: Seats are assigned but the whole team shifts to a different block of desks at fixed intervals through the year.

problems.1: The reorganization comes out of the same budget line that has not been raised since the team was half this size. I would rather know what this floor actually costs us, one way and every month, before we commit to a shape for it.
problems.2: My week is already cut into short gaps between meetings, and anything that eats those gaps costs far more than it looks like on paper. Before a layout is fixed I want to know what it takes out of our days, both while we are changing over and on every ordinary morning after.
problems.3: I sit still at one desk for most of eight hours, and by mid-afternoon how that spot sounds and how well it fits my body matter more to me than anything on the floor plan. Comfort is the part of this decision nobody ever writes down, and I would like it written down this time.
problems.4: Whatever we agree will hand some people a better place to sit than others, and as things stand that has never once been said out loud. I would rather we decided who carries the worse end of it than let it fall out of habit.
problems.5: Who I end up sitting beside decides how much of this team I actually talk to in a week, and right now that is being settled by furniture rather than by us. I would rather we worked out what that costs and what it buys now, not a year after the fact.

topic.title: Choosing where the group travels
topic.context: Five friends take one trip together each year and have reached the point where the destination must be fixed. Everyone is going regardless of which is chosen.

options.label: A
options.name: Hot Spring Town
options.summary: A stay at an inn in a spa town reachable by train, with meals taken at the inn and the days left unplanned.

options.label: B
options.name: City Break
options.summary: Several nights in a large city with separate accommodation and a loose plan, leaving each person to arrange their own daytime routes.

options.label: C
options.name: Island Trip
options.summary: A stay on an offshore island reached by ferry, with the group in one rented house and transport on the island arranged as a group.

problems.1: Whatever we settle on, the bill always lands differently from what I pictured when I agreed to it, and by then there is nothing to be done. I would rather know what the whole week costs before we commit than find it out in instalments.
problems.2: Every year the getting there swallows a day at each end, and I come home needing a rest from the holiday. What I mind is not the distance so much as how much of the week goes on arranging, moving and waiting.
problems.3: I sleep badly away from home, and it is the small things that decide how a week goes: where I wash, when I have to be at the table, whether there is anywhere to sit that is not a bed. By the middle of last year's trip I was counting the days.
problems.4: We have never had a rule for who pays for what, so it holds until it doesn't and somebody quietly ends up out of pocket. I would rather the money fell out of the arrangement itself than out of who happened to be organised that month.
problems.5: The point of these weeks is the five of us together, yet the last few have left me feeling either crowded or oddly alone, and never for a reason I could name at the time. Before we book anything I would like to understand what actually produces that.

topic.title: Dividing the utility bills
topic.context: The five people in a shared house have been splitting gas, water, and electricity in a way that was agreed when only three of them lived there. They are deciding how the bills will be divided from now on.

options.label: A
options.name: Per-Room Metering
options.summary: Individual meters are fitted to the private rooms, and each person settles their own reading while the shared-area consumption is billed to the household as a whole.

options.label: B
options.name: Flat Household Share
options.summary: The total is divided by the number of residents each month, with the amount recalculated whenever someone moves in or out of the house.

options.label: C
options.name: Seasonal Fixed Rate
options.summary: A set monthly figure is agreed in advance for each season, and the difference against the actual bills is settled once at the end of the year.

problems.1: The utilities envelope has stopped bearing any relation to what I put aside for it, and in the cold months my share lands like a second rent. I do not want to commit to anything before I know what the money actually does across a year, and what changing the setup would cost us up front.
problems.2: Working out what everyone owes has quietly become a monthly job that lands on whoever is least able to say no, and it takes longer every time someone queries it. Whatever we settle on, somebody has to keep it running, and I want to know how much of their evenings it will really swallow.
problems.3: I have started doing arithmetic in my head before switching anything on, and last winter I sat here in a coat rather than be the one who turned the heating up. What we choose will quietly decide how this place feels to live in, and I would rather that were said aloud than discovered in February.
problems.4: The way we divide this was worked out when the house was two-thirds full, and it now asks exactly the same of people whose days here look nothing alike. I keep hearing that somebody is carrying somebody else, and I would rather establish whether that is true than let it fester as a rumour.
problems.5: Money has started to sour how we speak to each other here: a reminder gets read as an accusation, and whoever sends it is avoided for a week afterwards. I would rather look squarely at where the bills have already damaged things between us than keep smoothing it over.

topic.title: Setting the membership fee structure
topic.context: A club's running costs have shifted since the fee was last set, and the five people on the committee must fix the structure for the coming year. Every member will pay under whichever structure is chosen.

options.label: A
options.name: Flat Annual Fee
options.summary: One figure charged to every member at the start of the year, covering all activities, with no separate charges collected during the year.

options.label: B
options.name: Activity-Based Charging
options.summary: A small base fee plus a charge attached to each event, collected from the members who take part in that particular event.

options.label: C
options.name: Tiered Membership
options.summary: Members choose between named levels of participation at the point of joining, each level carrying its own fee and its own scope of activities.

problems.1: The account is thinner than it looks, and I keep being asked what next year will actually cost people, yet nobody on the committee can say what we can count on coming in. I would rather not set a figure by guesswork the way we did last time.
problems.2: Keeping the books has swallowed whole evenings for whoever holds the job, and two people have handed the role back in three years. Before we commit to a way of collecting, I want to know what we are really asking of the next person who takes it on.
problems.3: The evenings have a hesitancy about them that was not there before, and several regulars now leave it until the last moment to decide whether to come out. Turning up to something you belong to should not need that much weighing up.
problems.4: The same dozen faces are at everything while others pay the same and appear twice a year, and it is being said openly now rather than muttered. I would rather find out how uneven it actually is, and who is carrying the work, before we argue about it.
problems.5: What has held this place together is that nobody knows or minds what anyone else puts in, and newcomers have always been able to drift in and find their feet. Both of those feel like they are slipping, and whatever we settle on will be visible to every member.

topic.title: Allocating the bicycle parking spaces
topic.context: A small apartment building has fewer bicycle spaces than residents who want them, and the five members of the residents' association must decide how they are allocated.

options.label: A
options.name: Annual Lottery
options.summary: All spaces are drawn by lot once a year among the households that apply, with the result standing until the next draw regardless of circumstances.

options.label: B
options.name: Paid Allocation
options.summary: Spaces are attached to a monthly charge and held by whoever takes them up, with the income going to the building's shared account.

options.label: C
options.name: Shared Racks
options.summary: The fixed allocation is dropped in favour of open double-tier racks that anyone may use on arrival, with no space belonging to a particular household.

problems.1: Every proposal that comes up at our meetings ends with someone asking what it will cost the building, and nobody has ever gone and looked. I also have no idea what a household actually pays when it ends up with nowhere to keep a bike.
problems.2: Whatever we settle on, somebody has to keep it running month after month, and the last two jobs we invented landed on one person and then quietly lapsed. I wanted to know what handling it would actually take, in paperwork and in physical effort.
problems.3: Getting a bike out in the morning has turned into a shoving match down there, and where yours happens to end up standing seems to decide what state it is in by the evening. Neither of those is anyone's fault exactly, which is why I went and looked properly.
problems.4: People have started grumbling that the same places always seem to go to the same doors, and I cannot tell whether that is how it actually happened or just resentment. Nor can I say whether the places we have now sit anywhere near where the bikes actually are.
problems.5: The last thing I want is a rule that turns people who currently nod at each other in the lobby into people who time their exits to avoid it. Things down in the bike area have gone sour once or twice already, and I wanted to know what happens to a building when an arrangement like this starts to bite.

topic.title: Deciding what the break room is for
topic.context: A shared room next to a small office has been used for several purposes at once, and it can no longer serve all of them. The five people who use it are settling its use.

options.label: A
options.name: Quiet Room
options.summary: The room is kept for individual rest with conversation and calls taken elsewhere, and the furniture is arranged for people sitting alone.

options.label: B
options.name: Meeting Space
options.summary: The room becomes bookable for small discussions, with a table and a screen installed and a shared calendar governing its use.

options.label: C
options.name: Open Kitchen
options.summary: The room is fitted out for preparing and eating food, with the appliances and storage maintained by whoever uses them.

problems.1: Whatever we settle on, somebody has to sign for it, and we are already paying out month by month because that room will not do the one thing we keep needing it for. I would rather see the figures on paper before we agree to anything.
problems.2: Every arrangement this building has tried ends up eating somebody's hours, either in upkeep that nobody actually volunteered for or in the walking about it leaves the rest of us doing. Before we commit to anything I want to know where those hours really go.
problems.3: I sit two metres from that door all day, and so does everyone else, and what happens in there does not stay in there. The complaints I hear are never about principle; they are about sound and mess, so I went and looked at both.
problems.4: Nobody ever decided how that room gets used; it simply goes to whoever gets there first, and the clearing up afterwards lands on whoever minds the most. I did not want to argue about any of that from impressions alone.
problems.5: We work a few metres apart and have somehow ended up strangers to one another, and when something difficult does need saying there is nowhere to say it. Whatever we choose has to be judged on that as much as on the fittings.

topic.title: Deciding how the shared car is used
topic.context: Five people share one vehicle that was bought jointly, and the informal arrangement has started to break down. They are settling how it is used and paid for.

options.label: A
options.name: Booking Calendar
options.summary: Use is reserved in advance through a shared calendar, with running costs divided according to the distance recorded for each booking.

options.label: B
options.name: Fixed Day Allocation
options.summary: Each person is allotted particular days of the week, holds the vehicle on those days whether or not they use it, and pays a fixed monthly share.

options.label: C
options.name: Primary Keeper
options.summary: One person keeps the vehicle and covers its running costs, and the others arrange use with that person and contribute per trip.

problems.1: Money for this car has been running on guesswork: someone shoves fuel in, a bill lands and whoever opens the envelope pays it, and none of us could say what a year of it comes to. Before we tie ourselves to any way of paying, I want the real figures and an honest picture of who has been doing the driving.
problems.2: Every use of this car costs an evening of arranging before it costs any fuel, and then someone has to untangle afterwards who owes what, usually whoever runs out of patience first. I wanted to see where those hours actually go before we sign up to another year of it.
problems.3: On an ordinary day this car is either not where I expected it or not in a state I would want to drive off in, and the things I count on it for are the first to fall over. What matters to me is how it feels to use on a plain midweek morning, not who is nominally in charge of it.
problems.4: Whatever we settle on will decide who quietly subsidises whom, and everything we have improvised so far leaned on the comfortable idea that a share is a share. I would rather know what an even split here would actually have to take into account.
problems.5: The car has started showing up in how we speak to each other, clipped replies, a favour asked once too often, and a fortnight where nobody mentioned it at all. Before we settle anything I want to know what actually sours groups like ours, our own past attempts included, so that we do not just move the sore point somewhere else.
